'''''Leymus arenarius''''' is a [[psammophilic]] ([[sand]]-loving) species of grass in the family [[Poaceae]], native to the coasts of Atlantic and Northern [[Europe]]. ''Leymus arenarius'' is commonly known as '''sand ryegrass''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=LEAR11|taxon=Leymus arenarius|accessdate=2 June 2015}}</ref> '''sea lyme grass''', or simply '''lyme grass'''.<ref name=can>[http://www.nunavuttourism.com/communities.php?cid=24 Sankiliuaq.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714213245/http://www.nunavuttourism.com/communities.php?cid=24 |date=2011-07-14 }} ''Canada's Arctic: Nunavut.'' (retrieved 16 March 2009)</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Leymus arenarius'' originated from the hybridization of ''L. racemosus'' and another unknown species in central Eurasia or from a polyploidization event.<ref name=Mizianty>{{Cite journal|title = Variability and structure of natural populations of Hordelymus europaeus (L.) Jess. ex Harz and Leymus arenarius (L.) Hochst. as revealed by morphology and DNA markers|last1 = Mizianty|first1 = M|date = 2007-10-18|journal = Plant Systematics and Evolution|volume = 269|issue = 1–2|pages = 15–28|doi = 10.1007/s00606-007-0586-2|last2 = Frey|first2 = L|last3 = Bieniek|last4 = Boron|last5 = Szklarczyk|first3 = W|first4 = P|first5 = M| bibcode=2007PSyEv.269...15M |s2cid = 7547705}}</ref> DNA analysis shows that inland and coastal plants are statistically not different from each other. ''L. arenarius'' is a relatively recent cultivar and has had little time to accumulate genetic differences.{{clarify|reason=differences from?|date=February 2016}} ''Leymus arenarius'' is much younger than its North American relative ''[[Leymus mollis|L. mollis]]'', which has been around since the Ice Age. Icelandic ''L. arenarius'' is molecularly uniform, and Polish ''L. arenarius'' is also reported to be molecularly uniform.<ref name=Mizianty/>

==Distribution==
''Leymus arenarius'' is native to the coasts of northern and western Europe. A closely related species, ''[[Leymus mollis]]'' (previously ''Elymus arenarius'' ssp. ''mollis'') is native to the northern coasts of North America.

==Growth and development==

===Nitrogen===
''Leymus arenarius'' can grow exponentially in terms of height and root development in the presence of nitrogen. ''L. arenarius'' is known to take up nitrogen into its root system. Increasing nitrogen concentrations can promote growth, as over time, the plant mass above the surface may not change, but nitrogen will accumulate in the root system. The roots themselves also retain nitrogen as they come in contact with it and the surrounding un-vegetated areas. This process aids in primary succession with surrounding flora and fauna, and helps reduce soil erosion. After volcanic events, ''L. arenarius'' contributes to the growth of dunes and their soil depth over time.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Accumulation of nitrogen and organic matter during primary succession of ''Leymus arenarius'' dunes on the volcanic island Surtsey, Iceland|url = http://www.biogeosciences.net/11/5763/2014/|journal = Biogeosciences|pages = 5763–5771|volume = 11|issue = 20|doi = 10.5194/bg-11-5763-2014|first1 = G.|last1 = Stefansdottir|first2 = A. L.|last2 = Aradottir|first3 = B. D.|last3 = Sigurdsson|year = 2014|bibcode = 2014BGeo...11.5763S|doi-access = free}}</ref> Nitrogen also increases seed production, raising the seed yield by as much as 70% in Icelandic ''L. arenarius''. Seed density also increases with the addition of nitrogen, in comparison to phosphorus and potassium, which only produce marginal increases in both seed yield and density. Leaf size and density are similarly influenced by nutrient additions. Removing nitrogen, phosphorus, or potassium resulted in a reduction of leaf mass by up to 20%. Nitrogen usage is a cost-effective strategy to increase abundance and effectiveness of ''L. arenarius''.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Responses of Leymus arenarius to Nutrients: Improvement of Seed Production and Seedling Establishment for Land Reclamation|jstor = 2405229|journal = Journal of Applied Ecology|date = 1997-10-01|pages = 1165–1176|volume = 34|issue = 5|doi = 10.2307/2405229|first1 = S.|last1 = Greipsson|first2 = A. J.|last2 = Davy| bibcode=1997JApEc..34.1165G }}</ref>

===Fungi===
''Leymus arenarius'' benefits from the presence of [[Mycorrhiza|arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi]]. The presence of the fungi increases the ability of ''L. arenarius'' to have an extensive root system and to bind soil particles. When adding fungi in its natural habitat, more seeds survived and grew than without the fungi present.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Inoculation of Grass and Tree Seedlings Used for Reclaiming Eroded Areas in Iceland with Mycorrhizal Fungi|jstor = 25133983|journal = Folia Geobotanica|date = 2003-06-01|pages = 209–222|volume = 38|issue = 2|first1 = Batkhuugyin|last1 = Enkhtuya|first2 = Úlfur|last2 = Óskarsson|first3 = John C.|last3 = Dodd|first4 = Miroslav|last4 = Vosátka|doi=10.1007/bf02803153| bibcode=2003FolGe..38..209E |s2cid = 25512316}}</ref>

===Adaptability===
''Leymus arenarius'' can easily adapt to a highly salinized area. When comparing the salt tolerances of Icelandic populations to the inland populations, the Icelandic populations exhibit a higher tolerance to salt. The trait for salt tolerance is heritable. The seeds of Icelandic populations germinated more effectively in the presence of  high salt concentration compared to seeds from inland population. In Finland the same salinity tolerance is observed near roadsides, where salt is distributed every season during snowfall. The pH near roadsides is similar to the pH found near saltwater beaches.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = A Rapid Adaptation to Low Salinity of Inland-Colonizing Populations of the Littoral Grass Leymus arenarius|jstor = 2475131|journal = International Journal of Plant Sciences|date = 1997-01-01|pages = 73–78|volume = 158|issue = 1|first1 = S.|last1 = Greipsson|first2 = H.|last2 = Ahokas|first3 = S.|last3 = Vähämiko|doi=10.1086/297415|s2cid = 84956155}}</ref>

==Pathogene resistance==
''Leymus arenarius'' has strong immunity to pathogens. A total of 160 transcripts for antimicrobial peptides are present in seedlings, with 30 transcripts encoding unique antimicrobial peptides. These peptides are not found in other plant species, and contribute to the plant's immune system, enhancing its resistance to wider range of pathogens compared to its relatives.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Prediction of Leymus arenarius (L.) antimicrobial peptides based on de novo transcriptome assembly|journal = Plant Molecular Biology|date = 2015-09-14|issn = 0167-4412|pages = 203–214|volume = 89|issue = 3|doi = 10.1007/s11103-015-0346-6|pmid = 26369913|first1 = Anna A.|last1 = Slavokhotova|first2 = Andrey A.|last2 = Shelenkov|first3 = Tatyana I.|last3 = Odintsova|s2cid = 8623809}}</ref>

==Uses==
In Europe, the plant's stems are used for roof thatching and can be woven into a coarse fabric. The seeds were historically used as food. As early as the 18th century, the plant's extensive network of roots was utilized to stabilizing sands on northern coastal beaches.<ref name=lyme>[http://www.plantguide.org/sea-lyme-grass.html Sea Lyme Grass.] ''Plant Guide.'' (retrieved 11 April 2009)</ref> In [[Iceland]], the grass was harvested as a wild grain as early as the 12th century.<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Nesbitt |first1=Mark |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=47 |isbn=0415927463}}</ref>

==Law==
During the 17th century, under the reign of [[William III of England|William III]], the Scottish Parliament passed a law protecting ''Leymus arenarius''. In the 18th century, during the reign of [[George I of Great Britain|George'' ''I]], the British Parliament expanded this law to protect the plant along English coasts. The law even declared the cutting or possession of the grass to be a penal offense.<ref name=lyme/>
